text: Lesson 10 defined the problem. This lesson builds the actual circuit that solves it — four steps, each doing exactly one job, ending with the inverse QFT from Chapter 2 reading the answer straight off the counting register.

Phase estimation uses two registers: n counting qubits, all starting at zero, and a target register holding U's eigenvector. Step one, Hadamard every counting qubit into a uniform superposition. Step two, for each counting qubit k, apply a controlled-U to the power of 2 to the k gate. Step three, apply the inverse quantum Fourier transform to the counting register. Step four, measure — the resulting n-bit string is your estimate of theta.

The mechanism behind step two is phase kickback. Take one control qubit in a uniform superposition and a target register in eigenstate psi with eigenvalue e to the i phi. Applying controlled-U does nothing when the control is zero and applies U when the control is one. Factoring psi back out of both terms shows the target register comes out completely unchanged, still exactly psi — the phase has been kicked back onto the control qubit instead, turning its superposition into a phase-shifted one.

One control qubit only gives one bit's worth of information, so phase estimation runs this kickback n times, with counting qubit k controlling U to the power of 2 to the k instead of U itself — repeated squaring that multiplies theta by that same power. The full counting register ends up in exactly the form a quantum Fourier transform produces when encoding a phase, which is why step three is QFT inverse: it decodes theta back into a bit string. For the exact case theta equals one quarter with n equals 2, this comes out fully deterministic — the probability of measuring k equals 1 is exactly 1.000000, and every other outcome is exactly zero.
Next lesson is the honest version: what phase estimation actually returns when theta doesn't land exactly on the grid, and what it costs to fix that.
